A final answer records whether a problem was solved. A reasoning trace records one route through the problem. That extra structure can teach useful decompositions, support verification, or merely make an incorrect answer sound systematic. This lecture treats a trace as data whose value must be established experimentally.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture, you should be able to:

1. distinguish answer supervision from process supervision;
2. compare chain-of-thought prompting, self-consistency, and self-training;
3. separate outcome reward models from process reward models;
4. design a verifier-guided test-time compute experiment; and
5. audit reasoning traces for correctness, faithfulness, and cost.

## From answers to traces

[Chain-of-thought prompting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.11903) [@wei2022cot] asks the model to produce intermediate text before its answer. The trace can expose a reusable method, but it is not guaranteed to be the mechanism that caused the prediction. A trace may contain a correct answer after an invalid step, a post-hoc explanation, or unnecessary tokens.

The training record should therefore keep several fields separate:

```text
problem | sampled trace | extracted answer | outcome | step labels | verifier version
```

This makes it possible to train on answers, traces, verified steps, or combinations without silently changing the dataset.

## Sampling and self-improvement

[Self-consistency](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.11171) [@wang2023selfconsistency] samples several reasoning paths and aggregates their answers. It is a test-time procedure: a fair comparison reports the number of samples, tokens, latency, and aggregation rule.

[STaR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.14465) [@zelikman2022star] turns successful model-generated rationales into new training data. Its loop is simple:

```text
sample traces → verify final answers → retain or rationalize successes
      → fine-tune → sample again
```

The danger is equally simple: selection can narrow the problem distribution, reward accidental shortcuts, and reinforce the model's preferred style rather than a general solution method.

## Outcome and process supervision

An **outcome reward model** scores a completed solution. A **process reward model** scores intermediate steps. Outcome labels are cheaper and often objectively checkable; process labels can identify the first invalid transition and provide denser feedback.

[Let's Verify Step by Step](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.20050) [@lightman2023verify] provides a central comparison between these supervision choices. The scientific question is not whether more labels help. It is which label granularity improves solution selection under matched annotation and inference budgets.

## Test-time compute as an experimental axis

A system can spend additional inference compute by generating longer traces, sampling more candidates, using a verifier to rerank them, or searching over partial solutions. Report a curve, not one score:

$$
Q(B)=\text{quality achieved under inference budget }B.
$$

Useful budgets include generated tokens, candidate count, verifier calls, latency, and monetary cost. The same model may dominate at one budget and lose at another.

## Studio: build a compute–quality curve

Use one fixed checkpoint and a held-out set of mathematical or symbolic tasks. Compare direct answering, one chain of thought, majority vote over several traces, and verifier reranking. Record exact-match accuracy, malformed-output rate, mean generated tokens, verifier calls, latency, and bootstrap confidence intervals.

The deliverable is a plot of quality against inference budget plus five inspected disagreements. The analysis must state whether the verifier finds genuinely better reasoning or only a more recognizable answer format.

## What to remember

1. Reasoning traces are supervision candidates, not ground truth about cognition.
2. Outcome and process labels trade annotation cost against diagnostic resolution.
3. Sampling, verification, and search spend different forms of test-time compute.
4. Reasoning claims require quality–budget curves and inspected failures.
5. The next lecture asks how verifiable rewards can change the policy itself.
